title: Efficient Discriminative Joint Encoders for Large Scale Vision-Language Reranking
claim: Expensive visual feature extraction dominates inference cost in joint encoders; ours cuts joint-encoding time dramatically while keeping accuracy competitive.
layout: 2 panels side-by-side: stacked horizontal bars left, accuracy-vs-time scatter right with ×53 annotation
description: Two plots side by side. Panel (a), "Inference time breakdown", is a horizontal stacked bar chart for ALBEF, BLIP (ViT-B), BLIP (ViT-L) and BLIP-2. Each bar is mostly dark navy for ViT feature extraction, with a small green segment for joint encoding. The ViT-L bars reach about 1450 ms and the ViT-B bars about 450 ms. Panel (b), "Retrieval vs. encoding time", is a scatter plot of Flickr image retrieval R@1 against joint-encoding inference time on a log axis. Points are colored by method: purple EDJE (Ours), pink ALBEF, blue BLIP and green BLIP-2. The EDJE points sit far left at high accuracy. A dashed gray line with a red "×53" label marks the speedup over BLIP ViT-L. The eye goes first to the dominant navy bars, then to the purple points and the red ×53.
caption: Inference efficiency and retrieval performance. (a) Methods with strong discriminative capabilities are dominated by costly ViT feature extraction, prohibiting their practical use for re-ranking. (b) EDJE achieves competitive zero-shot retrieval performance with up to 53× faster inference. Its token compression makes storing visual features practical, enabling large-scale retrieval.
abstract: Multimodal retrieval still leans on embedding-based models like CLIP for fast vector search over pre-computed image embeddings. Yet, unlike text retrieval, where joint-encoder rerankers are standard, comparable vision-language rerankers are largely absent. We find that seminal joint encoders such as BLIP are severely bottlenecked by an expensive visual feature-extraction stage, preventing practical deployment at scale. Motivated by this bottleneck, we introduce EDJE, an Efficient Discriminative Joint Encoder that precomputes vision tokens offline and compresses them via a lightweight attention-based adapter, so online inference runs only a compact joint encoder over a small set of visual tokens plus the text. EDJE preserves strong retrieval performance while drastically reducing storage and online compute, enabling high-throughput inference. Specifically, EDJE processes 50k image--text pairs/second while requiring 49kB of disk storage per image, matching prior art on Flickr (zero-shot) and COCO (fine-tuned) retrieval.
